overview:
Sayogi-kevali (Sanskrit: सयोगिकेवलिन्; often given in Prakrit as sayogikevalī or sayogikevalin) is a highly technical term in Jain doctrine describing an omniscient being (kevalin) who still retains activity (yoga) of body, speech, and mind. The word is formed from sa-yoga (with activity) and kevalin (one who has attained kevala-jñāna, omniscience). In the standard Jain analysis of the spiritual path, this state corresponds to the thirteenth guṇasthāna, the penultimate stage before complete cessation of all activity and final liberation.

Within the broader framework of Jain epistemology, kevala-jñāna is the fifth and highest type of knowledge, characterized as infinite, unobstructed, and all-comprehensive. A kevalin knows all substances (dravya), their infinite modes (paryāya), and the entirety of space and time—past, present, and future—without limitation. However, Jain philosophers distinguish between two modes of such omniscience: sayogi-kevali, in which omniscience is present while bodily, verbal, and mental activities continue; and ayogi-kevali, in which all such activities have ceased and the soul is on the verge of final disembodiment and liberation.

In the thirteenth guṇasthāna, called sayogikevali-guṇasthāna, the soul has destroyed the knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, deluding, and energy-obstructing karmas (the ghātiyā karmas), thereby attaining kevala-jñāna. Yet the non-destructive karmas related to body and lifespan (aghātiyā karmas) still remain, so the kevalin continues to exist in a physical body, can move, speak, and engage in teaching. This is the stage in which tīrthaṅkaras and other omniscient beings preach the doctrine and establish the fourfold community.

Classical works such as Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra describe the sayogikevali stage as the point at which all karmas become ready for dissolution and the third type of pure meditation (śukladhyāna) is practiced. The duration of this stage is said to range from an antarmuhūrta (a very short, sub-day interval) at minimum to something less than a koṭi of pūrvas at maximum, indicating that the period of active omniscience can be extremely brief or cosmically long depending on the specific karmic configuration of the soul.

Later philosophical texts, such as Haribhadra Sūri’s Anekāntajayapatākā, explicitly contrast sayogikevalin with ayogikevalin. The sayogikevalin is an omniscient being who has not yet given up any of the three yogas (activities of body, speech, and mind), whereas the ayogikevalin is an omniscient being on a higher plane, in the fourteenth guṇasthāna, who has stopped all activities, even mental ones. This distinction is important for Jain discussions of how an omniscient being can still function as a teacher and how liberation is finally attained.

From the perspective of sectarian traditions, both Digambara and Śvetāmbara schools accept the basic distinction between an omniscient being who still has activity and one who has completely ceased activity, though they differ on details of how a kevalin behaves. Digambara authors often emphasize that a kevalin, especially in the ayogi state, does not experience hunger or thirst and remains motionless, emitting a divine sound (divyadhvani) interpreted by disciples. Śvetāmbara authors, while also affirming the cessation of karmic bondage, allow for more explicit movement and preaching by the kevalin during the sayogi-kevali stage. In both cases, sayogi-kevali marks the living, embodied omniscient teacher, whereas ayogi-kevali marks the final, silent transition to liberation.

In doctrinal terms, the concept of sayogi-kevali helps clarify that omniscience in Jainism is not identical with immediate physical death or disembodiment. A soul can attain perfect knowledge while still inhabiting a body and engaging in the world, but this engagement is entirely non-attached and free from delusion. The kevalin’s activities are no longer causes of new karmic bondage; instead, they are the final unfolding of previously bound karmas. Thus, sayogi-kevali represents the culmination of the path of spiritual purification, where the omniscient being serves as a guide for others while awaiting the exhaustion of remaining karmas and the transition to ayogi-kevali and ultimate liberation (mokṣa).

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra
primary_sources.original_text: सयोगिकेवलि-गुणस्थानं तु तस्मिन् केवली भवति, तत्र तीर्थकृत्नामकर्मोदयः, सर्वे कर्मप्रभावा अपवृत्त्युपगमिनः। तृतीयं शुक्लध्यानं तत्र प्रवर्तते।
primary_sources.transliteration: sayogikevali-guṇasthānaṃ tu tasmin kevalī bhavati, tatra tīrthakṛtnāmakarmodayaḥ, sarve karmaprabhāvā apavṛttyupagaminaḥ. tṛtīyaṃ śukladhyānaṃ tatra pravartate.
primary_sources.translation: In the sayogikevali guṇasthāna he becomes a kevalin, and at that time the tīrthakṛt-nāma-karma may arise. All karmas then become ready for dissolution. The third (pure) meditation is practiced there.
primary_sources.notes:
This passage, summarized in modern scholarship, describes the thirteenth guṇasthāna as the stage of sayogi-kevali, where omniscience is attained and all karmas are poised for destruction. It situates sayogi-kevali within the larger narrative of the lives of the sixty-three illustrious persons and the technical doctrine of guṇasthānas.
Source tier: B–C (traditional commentary and scholarly summary based on Hemacandra’s text).

primary_sources.title: Anekāntajayapatākā-prakaraṇa
primary_sources.author: Haribhadra Sūri
primary_sources.original_text: सयोगिकेवलिन् नाम त्रयो योगान् न परित्यज्य तेरहगुणस्थानस्थितो केवली। अयोगिकेवलिन् पुनरयं चतुर्दशे गुणस्थाने सर्वयोगनिवृत्तिः।
primary_sources.transliteration: sayogikevalin nāma trayo yogān na parityajya terahaguṇasthānasthito kevalī. ayogikevalin punar ayaṃ caturdaśe guṇasthāne sarvayoganivṛttiḥ.
primary_sources.translation: A ‘sayogikevalin’ is an omniscient being who, without abandoning the three yogas, abides in the thirteenth guṇasthāna. An ‘ayogikevalin’, by contrast, is in the fourteenth guṇasthāna, where all yogas have ceased.
primary_sources.notes:
This definition, reported in secondary summaries of Haribhadra’s work, explicitly contrasts the sayogi-kevali with the ayogi-kevali and anchors both in the technical scheme of the fourteen guṇasthānas.
Source tier: B–C (traditional philosophical text accessed through scholarly summary).

primary_sources.title: Nandi Sūtra (on kevala-jñāna)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Devavācaka
primary_sources.original_text: जेण णं सव्वे दव्वा सव्वो लोओ तिहि कालेहि सव्वा परियायाः पस्यन्ति जाणन्ति तं केवलं णाणं।
primary_sources.transliteration: jeṇa ṇaṃ savve davvā savvo loao tihi kālehi savvā pariyāyā pasyanti jāṇanti taṃ kevalaṃ ṇāṇaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: That knowledge by which all substances, the entire universe, all three times, and all modes are seen and known—that is kevala-knowledge.
primary_sources.notes:
While this verse does not use the term sayogi-kevali, it defines kevala-jñāna, the omniscience that characterizes both sayogi-kevali and ayogi-kevali. Sayogi-kevali is the state in which this kevala-jñāna is present along with bodily, verbal, and mental activity.
Source tier: A–B (primary Prakrit text with traditional commentary).

misconceptions.myth: Sayogi-kevali is a lesser or imperfect form of omniscience compared to ayogi-kevali.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine holds that kevala-jñāna is identical in its infinitude and perfection in both sayogi-kevali and ayogi-kevali states. The distinction concerns the presence or absence of bodily, verbal, and mental activity (yoga), not the degree of omniscience. In the sayogi-kevali stage, the kevalin is fully omniscient but still embodied and active; in the ayogi-kevali stage, omniscience continues while all activity has ceased and liberation is imminent.

misconceptions.myth: A sayogi-kevali continues to accumulate new karmas through action and speech.
misconceptions.reality: By the time a soul reaches the sayogi-kevali stage, the destructive karmas that cause bondage and delusion have been annihilated. The remaining activities of body, speech, and mind are merely the final fruition of previously bound karmas and do not create new bondage. The kevalin’s actions are entirely non-attached and do not generate fresh karmic influx.

While Jain narratives focus on tīrthaṅkaras as paradigmatic sayogi-kevalins who preach and establish the community, the doctrinal category of sayogi-kevali is broader. Any soul that attains kevala-jñāna while still retaining activity of body, speech, and mind is, by definition, a sayogi-kevali, whether or not it functions as a tīrthaṅkara.
